But if bank queries share the same FORMAL->CASUAL shift the LoRA was trained on, the "popularity" estimate is biased toward the synthetic-query distribution, not the 30 real eval queries; mild distribution mismatch in the correction itself.
6) Combination order matters: apply on the SAME score space you report (frozen vs LoRA). Stacking MP on top of the LoRA scores is the only interesting test; on frozen scores it just re-tells the QB-Norm result.
7) Cosine-sim direction: implement with sims and "<" (less similar) as shown; do NOT convert to a Gaussian (the normal-distribution MP variant assumes Gaussian per-object distances, violated by 588 cosine sims on a tight fashion manifold) -- task's instinct to use the empirical/rank form is correct.

verdicts.name: k-reciprocal encoding rerank (Zhong et al., CVPR 2017) over the image-image gallery graph, candidate-preserving on top-20
verdicts.correct_mechanism:
REAL METHOD (Zhong, Zheng, Cao, Li, "Re-ranking Person Re-identification with k-reciprocal Encoding", CVPR 2017). Canonical formulation operates within ONE modality on a combined probe+gallery set.

Original method (per query/probe p, gallery G):
1. N(p,k) = the k nearest neighbors of p by original distance d (here cosine -> d = 1 - cos).
2. k-reciprocal set: R(p,k) = { g in N(p,k) : p in N(g,k) }  (mutual NN).
3. Expansion: for each q in R(p,k), if |R(p,k) ∩ R(q, k/2)| >= (2/3)|R(q, k/2)|, add R(q,k/2) into R*(p,k). Call result R*.
4. Encode each item as a sparse feature vector V_p over the whole set, weighted by a Gaussian kernel on original distance:
   V_p(g_i) = exp(-d(p,g_i)) if g_i in R*(p,k1), else 0; then L1-normalize V_p.
   (k1 builds the set; k2 is used in the next step.)
5. Local query expansion to denoise: V_p <- (1/k2) * sum over top-k2 neighbors g_j of p of V_{g_j}.
6. Jaccard distance between p and any gallery g, computed from the sparse encodings (min/max trick):
   d_J(p,g) = 1 - ( sum_i min(V_p(i), V_g(i)) ) / ( sum_i max(V_p(i), V_g(i)) ).
7. Final: d*(p,g) = (1 - lambda) * d_J(p,g) + lambda * d_original(p,g). Rank by d* ascending. Paper defaults k1=20, k2=6, lambda=0.3.

CRITICAL: the k-reciprocal sets and V vectors are normally computed in the SAME embedding space for probe and gallery (probe is an image; original ReID is image->image). The encoding requires d(probe, gallery_i) AND d(gallery_i, gallery_j) to live on one comparable scale.

ADAPTATION TO THIS T2I SETTING with Q (n,768 text, L2-norm), G (588,768 image, L2-norm), bank Qb (~7000,768 text):
Two incompatible variants exist; both are problematic.

VARIANT A (as VET proposed: image-image graph + cross-modal seed). For each text query q:
  s = q @ G.T  (1,588) text->image cosine; d_tq = 1 - s.
  Gd = 1 - G @ G.T (588,588) image-image cosine distance.
  Treat q as a pseudo-node whose only edges to gallery are d_tq, and gallery-gallery edges are Gd. Build R*(q,k1) from d_tq, build R*(g,k1) from Gd for each gallery g, encode V_q (from d_tq) and V_g (from Gd), then d_J + lambda blend, restricted to the top-20 candidate set (others kept below). 
  FLAW: V_q is built ONLY from cross-modal distances d_tq while V_g is built ONLY from intra-modal Gd. These two encodings live in different distance regimes (cross-modal cosines are systematically lower/flatter than intra-modal image-image cosines), so the min/max Jaccard overlap is dominated by scale mismatch, not semantics. The 'reciprocity' p in N(g,k) test is ill-defined because g's neighbor list is image-image but q's is cross-modal.

VARIANT B (mathematically clean: pull query INTO image space first via the LoRA text tower so q and G are co-embedded, then run STANDARD same-space k-reciprocal with probe=q over gallery G). This is the only version faithful to the paper. It still re-ranks top-20 candidate-preserving. d_original = d_tq; everything else standard with k1≈6-10 (NOT 20 — see gotchas), k2≈2-3, lambda≈0.7-0.85 (HIGH, per VET's own risk note).

RECOMMENDED IF TRIED AT ALL: Variant B, candidate-preserving over top-20, k1 small (6), k2=2, lambda=0.8, rank gold-safe (gold cannot leave top-20). But expectation of gain is low — see gotchas.
verdicts.gotchas:
BRUTALLY HONEST — why this likely does NOT help on N=30 single-positive T2I:

1. METHOD-TASK MISMATCH (fatal-ish): k-reciprocal re-ranking is designed for MANY-positive retrieval (ReID: one probe has multiple correct gallery shots of the same identity). Its entire benefit comes from propagating affinity through clusters of true positives that mutually reciprocate. With SINGLE positive per query and 588 distinct products, there is no positive cluster to exploit. The gold image has no 'siblings' in the gallery to reinforce it; its k-reciprocal set is filled with visually-similar-but-WRONG products. This is exactly the failure mode VET flagged, and it is the dominant effect here, not an edge risk.

2. ANTI-CORRECTIVE BIAS: image-image manifold smoothing pulls each candidate toward its visual neighbors. For top-wear that means near-duplicate products (same silhouette/color, different brand) get their scores tied together. If the gold is a slightly-off match the model ranked at position 3, k-reciprocal will happily promote its 4 look-alikes above it. On single-positive eval this directly threatens R@1 and MRR — the metrics that matter — even while it cannot drop gold below the top-20 cut (candidate-preserving only protects R@10, not R@1/MRR).

3. CROSS-MODAL SCALE MISMATCH (Variant A specifically): the VET-proposed image-image-graph-with-text-seed is not the real algorithm. Jaccard over encodings built from two different distance distributions is dominated by scale, not meaning. Variant A is methodologically broken; do not implement it. Only Variant B is defensible, and Variant B is 'just standard re-ranking', which weakens the novelty pitch.

4. NOVELTY CLAIM IS THIN: re-framed honestly, Variant B = run the textbook k-reciprocal re-rank with the query co-embedded via the existing LoRA. A reviewer can say 'you applied an off-the-shelf ReID re-ranker'; the only novel twist (image-image graph for a cross-modal query) is the broken Variant A. So the method that works isn't novel and the method that's novel doesn't work.

5. N=30 STATISTICAL FUTILITY: baseline MRR CIs are already very wide. k-reciprocal typically moves ReID mAP by a few points in many-positive regimes; here the expected effect is near-zero-or-negative and will be invisible inside the bootstrap CI. You cannot get a defensible 'beats baseline' claim out of a noise-level delta on N=30.

6. PARAMETER LANDMINE: paper default k1=20 over a 588-gallery with single positives is far too large — it will pull in ~20 wrong neighbors per node and over-smooth catastrophically. Must use tiny k1 (≈6) and high lambda (≈0.8), at which point the Jaccard term contributes almost nothing and you've effectively reverted to the original ranking. So the safe setting is the trivial setting.

7. RECIPROCITY SPARSITY: at lambda high / k small the reciprocal sets are tiny and often empty for the gold, so d_J degenerates to 1 for many pairs and adds pure noise to the blend.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE VERDICT: if the gallery actually contained multiple images per product (true positives clusters) this method would be a genuine fit. It does not (588 single items). Also if eval were multi-positive. Neither holds.

CHEAP SALVAGE if you insist on touching the image-image manifold: skip k-reciprocal entirely and just try a single graph-smoothing / k-NN local-query-expansion pass on the top-20 with very low weight — same family, less machinery — but expect the same single-positive demotion problem.
verdicts.citation_real: Zhong, Zheng, Cao, Li. "Re-ranking Person Re-identification with k-reciprocal Encoding." CVPR 2017. arXiv:1701.08398. ~3000+ citations — well above the ~100 bar; the method is unquestionably real and standard. (Note: I confirmed this from established knowledge; web tools returned no output in this session, but this paper and its formula are canonical and I am highly confident of the equations as given.)

verdicts.name: HyDE x query-bank kNN hybrid expansion (3-way GRF+PRF cross-modal fusion)
verdicts.correct_mechanism:
Both base methods CONFIRMED real; the adaptation is faithful.

- HyDE (Gao et al., ACL 2023, arXiv:2212.10496): LLM generates N hypothetical docs, encode each, final search vector averages them WITH the original query folded in: v_hat = (1/(N+1)) * [ g(q) + sum_{k=1..N} g(d_k) ]. g = encoder, d_k = N generated hypothetical docs.
- GRF+PRF complementarity CONFIRMED: Mackie, Chatterjee, Dalton, 'Generative and Pseudo-Relevance Feedback for Sparse, Dense and Learned Sparse Retrieval', SIGIR 2023, arXiv:2305.07477 -- explicitly finds GRF (LLM-generated) and PRF (top-k corpus) signals are COMPLEMENTARY and combine to further improve recall. Basis for w1*q + w2*HyDE + w3*PRF.

Adapted to single-positive T2I (all vectors verified L2-normalized, norm=1.0):
Index = shared__gallery_emb.npy = FROZEN VISION G (588,768) [NOT the *_doc caption embeddings]. Eval Q=(30,768) via LoRA text tower (current best). Query bank Qb=(7023,768) synthetic user-style queries, TEXT side.
- HyDE leg (needs vLLM, NOT cached): per q, prompt EXAONE/Qwen for N>=4 hypothetical formal Musinsa captions; encode with the SAME LoRA SigLIP2 text tower; hyde_i = L2(mean_k g(d_k)).
- bank-kNN/PRF leg (training-free, cached): S=Q@Qb.T; top-k idx_i; bank_i = L2(mean_{j in idx_i} Qb[j]).
- Fuse + retrieve: q'_i = L2(w1*Q[i] + w2*hyde_i + w3*bank_i); scores = q'@G.T; rank 588; R@1/5/10 + MRR; percentile bootstrap 95% CI (10k, resample 30).
Weights MUST be fixed on the 717-query VAL set against its OWN 240-product val gallery (shared__val_gallery_emb.npy, val_gt in meta.json), never on eval. Repo provides src/novel/lib.py (load_caches/ranks_of/metrics_from_ranks/bootstrap_ci/paired_compare/select_eval) -- use select_eval for honest val-tuning + paired tests. NOTE scipy is NOT installed in the jolnon env (paired_compare's sign-test will crash); use numpy-only paired bootstrap or pip install scipy.
verdicts.gotchas:
Measured on the REAL cache with the CORRECT frozen-vision index via src/novel/lib.py (run with /opt/miniconda3/envs/jolnon/bin/python3.11 -- only that interpreter has numpy). Baselines reproduce: EVAL frozen MRR=0.5711 [0.421,0.722], EVAL LoRA MRR=0.6842 [0.537,0.825].

1. bank-kNN/PRF leg is REAL but negligible and NOT significant at N=30. Tuned on val gallery (k=10,a=0.05; valMRR 0.7713->0.7722 = noise), applied to eval -> MRR=0.6900 (+0.0058 over LoRA). Paired bootstrap vs LoRA (numpy, 10k): delta=+0.0058, 95% CI [-0.0007,+0.0176] (straddles 0), P(d>0)=0.84, W2/L2/T26 -- only 4 of 30 queries move, net +0. The grid is robust (46/49 (k,a) configs beat LoRA, so not harmful) but the effect is within noise.

2. HyDE leg's realistic ceiling is barely above LoRA. Probed by substituting the gt's OWN caption-text embedding as a 'perfect' hypothetical caption: best-on-eval ceiling MRR=0.7083 (+0.024 vs LoRA), keeps w3=0.2 (bank leg not dead). Oracle ceiling (gt IMAGE as the term) = 1.000 but unreachable. The realistic ceiling is already cherry-picked on eval and a real LLM caption will land below the gt caption, so honest expected gain is ~0.

3. Cross-modal gap is the root cause. Index is IMAGE space; HyDE/PRF terms are TEXT. cos(gt_caption_text, gt_image)=0.106 vs cos(lora_query, gt_image)=0.145 -- a 'perfect' hypothetical caption points at the right image LESS well than the raw LoRA query. A text-space HyDE term adds text-cluster bias, not image-discriminative signal.

4. N=30 attribution is fatal for a 3-way weight method (the proposal itself ranked this last). 1 query rank5->1 = +0.0267 MRR; both legs' honest gains are < one query and inside the LoRA CI width (0.262). A (w1,w2,w3) grid over 30 single-positive queries is uninterpretable; CIs swallow it.

5. Redundancy: LoRA already maps casual->catalogue on the text side; bank-NN pulls toward the synthetic-query cluster LoRA trained on (little new signal); HyDE re-formalizes the query, partly undoing the casual->formal benefit.

6. Cost vs payoff: most moving parts (LLM gen + 3 weights) for the smallest, non-significant gain. The 2-way subset (q + bank-kNN, no HyDE) is fully cached, costs no LLM, and yields the same negligible effect -- so the HyDE leg adds cost without evidence.
verdicts.citation_real: REAL. HyDE: Gao, Ma, Lin, Callan, 'Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels', arXiv:2212.10496, ACL 2023 (final vector averages generated docs with f(q) included). GRF + GRF/PRF complementarity (linear interpolation of query with generative and pseudo-relevance terms): Mackie, Chatterjee, Dalton, 'Generative Relevance Feedback with Large Language Models', arXiv:2304.13157, SIGIR 2023; companion 'Generative and Pseudo-Relevance Feedback for Sparse, Dense and Learned Sparse Retrieval', arXiv:2305.07477 (states GRF and PRF are complementary and combine to improve recall).

survey_angle_summaries: Hubness - a small set of gallery items being the nearest neighbour of disproportionately many queries - is a well-documented pathology of high-dimensional dense/cross-modal retrieval (Radovanovic 2010) and is a strong, underexplored explanation for WHY your formal-caption gallery underserves casual queries: zero-shot SigLIP2 likely has caption-style 'hub' products that absorb many casual queries. The literature offers a clean family of TRAINING-FREE, test-time fixes that operate purely on cached cosine matrices plus a query set - which maps exactly onto your assets (frozen 588 gallery embeddings + ~7000 synthetic casual query bank). Ranked best-fit-for-you: (1) Dynamic Inverted Softmax / QB-Norm (CVPR 2022) is the headline - precompute querybank-vs-gallery sims, take a per-gallery column softmax (beta=20) as a hub weight, multiply into test-query sims, applied selectively (DIS) so non-hub queries are untouched; the synthetic bank IS the distribution-matched querybank, directly operationalising your core hypothesis. (2) CSLS (MUSE, ICLR 2018) is the simplest: subtract each gallery item's mean similarity to its K~10 nearest queries, score = 2cos - r_bank(y); pure arithmetic. (3) Mutual Proximity (JMLR 2012) gives a rank-based, doubly-symmetric classical baseline. (4) Local Scaling/NICDM and (5) Dual Softmax/Sinkhorn and (6) mean-centering / All-but-the-Top round out a cheap 'we surveyed hubness mitigation' comparison table. KEY HONESTY POINTS for our setting: (a) every query-side statistic must be estimated from the 7000-query bank, NEVER the 30 test queries, to avoid a fatal leakage critique; (b) with N=30 the per-method delta will often sit inside bootstrap CIs - report consistent point gains and per-difficulty-bucket effects (short_ambiguous queries are the ones most likely dominated by hubs) rather than claiming significance; (c) all of these compose with the existing LoRA text tower and run in seconds. Recommended path: lead with DIS (safe, novel-vs-your-current-methods, distribution-matched bank), include CSLS + Mutual Proximity as cheap comparison rows, and report hubness skewness reduction (skew of the k-occurrence distribution) as a mechanism-level metric to make the story defensible even when R@k CIs overlap. Tune all knobs (beta, K, tau) on a held-out slice of the query bank.

ANGLE: the CLIP/SigLIP modality gap (Liang et al., Mind the Gap, NeurIPS 2022) and training-free test-time corrections that reshape cached embeddings or rescale the similarity matrix to improve cross-modal retrieval with zero training. All methods below run in seconds-to-minutes on assets you already have (588 cached gallery image embeddings + the ~7000-query bank) and stack on either the frozen or LoRA text tower.

They split into two mechanistic families addressing two distinct failure modes:

(A) GEOMETRIC OFFSET / ANISOTROPY - the constant gap between the text and image cones plus dominant shared directions. Methods: per-modality mean-shift calibration (GR-CLIP, 2025), gap-vector shift with swept lambda (Mind the Gap, NeurIPS 2022), and All-but-the-Top mean+top-PC removal / whitening (ICLR 2018). These directly operationalize the project's core hypothesis (casual-query vs formal-caption distribution offset) as a measurable, removable direction - estimate the text mean from the query bank and the image mean from the gallery. This is the single most on-thesis, lowest-effort, highest-credibility intervention.

(B) HUBNESS / SCORE-DISTRIBUTION SKEW - a few gallery images that are near-neighbors of almost every query dominate the top ranks. Methods: DBNorm dual-bank dynamic inverted softmax (EMNLP 2023; uses query bank + gallery bank, exactly our assets, +7.6 R@1 reported on MSCOCO), QB-Norm/Dynamic Inverted Softmax (CVPR 2022; single bank), and classical hubness reduction (Mutual Proximity, Local Scaling/NICDM; JMLR 2012, off-the-shelf in scikit-hubness). These rescale the similarity matrix using bank statistics and attack a different mechanism than family A, so they can compose with it.

A fourth, more novel-but-pricier option is modality inversion (Cross the Gap, ICLR 2025): optimize a per-query pseudo-embedding in image space before retrieval. It is the most novel but does NOT run purely on cached embeddings (needs the text encoder in the loop) - treat as a stretch goal.

RECOMMENDED SEQUENCING for the fastest defensible win:
1. Modality-gap calibration as ONE combined study: per-modality mean subtraction with a tunable lambda (methods 1+2+3 framed together), lambda/D tuned on the query bank. Lowest effort, most on-thesis, anchored to a top-tier citation.
2. ONE hubness method, primary = DBNorm dynamic dual-bank (method 4) since you already have both banks; keep QB-Norm and MP/LS as baselines inside that same study, not separate wins.
3. Compose A + B (calibrate embeddings, then bank-normalize the matrix) for a stacked result.

HONESTY CAVEATS FOR THIS EXACT SETTING: (i) the gap effect is NON-MONOTONIC - fully closing the gap can hurt; lambda/D/tau/beta/k must all be tuned on the query bank, never the 30 eval queries (defensibility floor). (ii) Family-B methods overlap heavily (all inverted-softmax / hubness family) - pick one primary to avoid claiming redundant wins. (iii) Gains may be capped because LoRA already partially shifts the text cone (it does some of what mean-shift does) and the 588-item gallery limits how severe hubness can be. (iv) With N=30, every claim needs bootstrap CIs; per-query swings are large. The safest single addition is mean-shift calibration + DBNorm composed, both validated on the held-out query bank and reported with bootstrap CIs.

Pseudo-relevance feedback (PRF) and query expansion map unusually well onto this setting because SigLIP2 gives a single L2-normalized cosine space shared by the cached image embeddings, the query, the LoRA text tower, and the 7000-query bank, so almost every classic PRF operation reduces to cheap vector arithmetic on assets that already exist, with no training and runtimes in milliseconds. The angle splits into three families. (1) Cross-modal/visual PRF (Rocchio/Vector-PRF, alpha-QE, iterative gated PRF, database-side augmentation): refine the query or denoise the gallery by averaging top-k retrieved IMAGE vectors into the query, training-free on cached embeddings; the central risk is query drift since single-positive top-k is noisy, which the confidence-gated and cosine-weighted (alpha-QE) variants explicitly counter. (2) Generative expansion (HyDE, GRF, CuPL-style prompt ensembling): use the local EXAONE/Qwen LLMs to turn a casual Korean query into formal pseudo-captions or paraphrase ensembles, encode with the SigLIP2 text tower, and average -- this is the most on-thesis family because it directly transports the casual query into the FORMAL-caption distribution the index was built on, attacking the project's core hypothesis with no API and no training. (3) Query-bank retrieval-augmented expansion: treat the 7000 synthetic queries as a query log and snap each test query toward its embedding-space neighbors, regularizing it onto the exact distribution the LoRA was trained on -- a near-free win that current methods underuse. My ranked recommendations: start with HyDE (highest fit-to-hypothesis, ~700 cites, low effort) and query-bank kNN expansion (uses an existing asset, low effort), validate each alone with bootstrap CIs, then optionally combine them (HyDE x bank fusion, the GRF+PRF complementarity story) and add cross-modal Rocchio/alpha-QE as a secondary, gated layer. All are training-free, novel relative to the user's tried-and-crude list, and the dominant shared risk is overfitting hyperparameters to N=30 -- so all weights/k/alpha should be tuned on the query bank, never on the 30-query eval set.

Training-free, test-time reranking/calibration on the cached SigLIP2 similarity structure. The single best-fit family is QUERY-BANK NORMALIZATION (QB-Norm / Dynamic Inverted Softmax): the user already has ~7000 synthetic queries, exactly the asset QB-Norm needs, and it directly attacks the hubness that the formal-caption/casual-query gap produces (a few generic top-wear products becoming hubs for many casual queries). It is the highest-leverage, lowest-effort, most novel-vs-current idea here and runs in minutes on cached matrices. Secondary, complementary, also-training-free ideas operate on the gallery's intra-modal (image-image) manifold (k-reciprocal/Jaccard reranking, gallery diffusion, database-side augmentation) which the raw text->image cosine ignores. Dual-Softmax/Sinkhorn is powerful but TRANSDUCTIVE (uses the test-query batch) and would be an obvious defensibility critique with N=30 single-positive queries; it is included but flagged as risky and best replaced by the query-bank variant. Modality-gap centering is a cheap one-liner worth trying but unreliable. Overall: lead with QB-Norm/DIS on the query bank; layer a candidate-preserving k-reciprocal or gallery-DBA rerank of top-K as a second, orthogonal, novel signal. All methods are honestly fragile at N=30, so report bootstrap CIs and pick the variant that wins robustly rather than chasing the largest point gain.

Angle: synthetic-query generation for retrieval and its upgrades (Promptagator / InPars / Doc2Query, round-trip consistency filtering, query diversity, hard-negative mining), adapted to THIS SigLIP2 cached-embedding Korean fashion setting. The decisive fact about the project is that the user already generated a ~7000-query bank (train_pairs_final.jsonl; query_type 1 = short, query_type 2 = long, ~3 queries x 2 styles per ~1170 train products) and trains a text-only LoRA on essentially ALL of it RAW, with in-batch negatives only, no quality filtering and no hard negatives. The synthetic-data literature says that is exactly where the largest, cheapest, lowest-risk wins live -- and the project already has the assets to do them nearly for free: data/novel_cache/ holds base__ and lora384__ embeddings for gallery_doc (588), bank_q (~7000), eval_q (30) and val_q/val_doc, plus shared__gallery_emb. So consistency filtering, HyDE-style pooling and query-bank-prototype methods reduce to small matmuls that run in minutes with zero re-encoding (note: numpy is not in the default python env, so a venv/uv install is a one-line prerequisite). Eval is 30 single-positive queries in short_ambiguous/medium/long_specific buckets (gallery=588), so report bootstrap CIs and favor large-effect interventions.

Highest-leverage, most-novel-vs-current cluster = FILTER the bank that is currently used raw. (1) Promptagator-style CROSS-MODAL round-trip consistency filtering: keep a synthetic query only if its source product IMAGE is in top-K when its cached text embedding is scored against the 588 cached frozen vision embeddings; drop the off-topic/generic queries EXAONE/Qwen inevitably produced; retrain the same cheap LoRA on the filtered set, optionally iterate once. The filter is training-free and a ~7000x588 matmul on the existing cache. Confirmed from the paper: the retriever is trained on the synthetic data itself and a query is kept iff it retrieves its source passage in top-K; this 'removes ambiguous, generic, and low-quality questions and significantly improves retrieval'. (2) InPars-v2-style INDEPENDENT relevance filtering stacked on top (v2 replaced v1's generator log-prob filter with a monoT5-3B reranker score) -- here, use the already-deployed EXAONE/Qwen on vLLM as a pointwise relevance judge (semantic catch vs the embedding-space catch of #1).

Second cluster fixes the in-batch-negatives-only LoRA: (4) TripletCLIP-inspired mined hard negatives from cached vision-NN + minimal-attribute-edit captions (color/fit/neckline), made SAFE by (5) SimANS/RocketQA denoised 'ambiguous' sampling -- critical because a 588-product top-wear gallery has near-duplicates, so naive top-NN hard negatives are false negatives. This directly targets the fine-attribute discrimination the failed ColBERT/learned-reranker could not learn.

Third cluster is fully TRAINING-FREE and operationalizes the core formal-vs-casual hypothesis at TEST time on cached embeddings: (3) Reverse-HyDE -- LLM rewrites the casual Korean query into N formal catalogue-style captions, embed, mean-pool with the query, search the untouched cached vision embeddings; and (7) query-bank prototype pooling -- reuse the 7000 cached bank embeddings as a relevance-feedback manifold with no new generation. (6) DRAGON grounds a diversity/coverage rebalance of the bank to match the eval's short/medium/long taxonomy.

Recommended priority under one-week / speed-over-rigor: do #1 (round-trip filter + retrain) and #3 (Reverse-HyDE) first -- both cheap, novel vs the current crude pipeline, and defensible; add #4+#5 (denoised hard-negative LoRA) if more headroom is needed; #2/#6/#7 are stackable extras. Caveat for every method: N=30 with very wide bootstrap CIs means report CIs and prefer large-effect interventions (filtering, hard negatives) over marginal ones (prototype pooling).

From the fashion/e-commerce text-image retrieval literature, the highest-leverage, training-free moves for your cached-SigLIP2 + query-bank + local-LLM setting are LANGUAGE-SPACE BRIDGING and SIMILARITY-SPACE NORMALISATION, not new fine-tuning. The single best fit is HyDE-style query bridging (arXiv:2212.10496): have a local LLM rewrite each casual Korean query into a hypothetical FORMAL product caption, then embed that with the SigLIP2 text tower. This makes your core hypothesis (formal-caption vs casual-query gap) a test-time generation step instead of a LoRA, runs in seconds on the 30 eval queries, leaves the frozen gallery vision embeddings untouched, and composes with the existing LoRA. Its index-side mirror is CuPL/multi-caption gallery enrichment (arXiv:2209.03320): LLM-generate several varied-register descriptions per product, average their text embeddings into a parallel text index, and late-fuse with vision. A third, distinct lever you are uniquely positioned to use is QB-Norm Dynamic Inverted Softmax (arXiv:2112.12777), which exploits your ~7000-query bank to de-hub gallery items purely as a post-process on the cached similarity matrix. Recommended bets given speed-dominates-rigor and the wide N=30 bootstrap CIs: lead with HyDE (high gain, low effort), stack QB-Norm and/or CuPL enrichment, and keep query-ensembling/PRF as ablations.
